body.en: Arithmetic and geometric progressions, and the binomial expansion of \( (a+b)^{n} \).
AP sum \( S_n=\tfrac{n}{2}\big(2a+(n-1)d\big) \); GP sum \( S_n=\tfrac{a(1-r^{n})}{1-r} \); binomial \( (1+x)^{n}=1+nx+\tfrac{n(n-1)}{2}x^{2}+\cdots \).

label.en: ● Deep Conceptual Intuition — Series & the Binomial Theorem

body.en: Arithmetic, Geometric & Power Series Convergence: An arithmetic progression grows additively (\(u_n = a + (n-1)d\), \(S_n = \tfrac{n}{2}[2a + (n-1)d]\)), whereas a geometric progression scales multiplicatively (\(u_n = ar^{n-1}\), \(S_n = \dfrac{a(1-r^n)}{1-r}\)). An infinite geometric series \(\sum_{n=1}^\infty ar^{n-1}\) converges to \(S_\infty = \dfrac{a}{1-r}\) if and only if \(|r| < 1\). Similarly, the general binomial expansion \((1 + kx)^n = 1 + n(kx) + \dfrac{n(n-1)}{2!}(kx)^2 + \cdots\) for negative or fractional \(n\) converges if and only if \(|kx| < 1 \iff |x| < 1/|k|\).

body.en:
Convergence condition for \(S_\infty\): The sum to infinity \(S_\infty = \frac{a}{1-r}\) is valid if and only if \(|r| < 1\) (\(-1 < r < 1\)). If a question states that a series has a sum to infinity, you can establish an inequality for unknown parameters: \(-1 < r < 1\).

Binomial powers on coefficients: In \((a+bx)^n\), the term involving \(x^r\) contains \((bx)^r = b^r x^r\). Writing \(3x^2\) instead of \((3x)^2 = 9x^2\) or \(-2x^3\) instead of \((-2x)^3 = -8x^3\) destroys the coefficient.

Term formulas index offset: In an AP, the \(n\)-th term has \(n-1\) common differences: \(u_n = a + (n-1)d\). In a GP, \(u_n = ar^{n-1}\). Do not confuse the \(n\)-th term with the sum \(S_n\).

label.en: ◆ Why It Works — First-Principles Derivation (Series & the Binomial Theorem)

body.en:
Why the Geometric Sum Formula & \(S_\infty\) Work: Write \(S_n = a + ar + ar^2 + \dots + ar^{n-1}\). Multiplying through by \(r\) shifts every power up by one:

\[ S_n - rS_n = (a + ar + \dots + ar^{n-1}) - (ar + ar^2 + \dots + ar^n) = a - ar^n \]

Factoring \(S_n(1 - r) = a(1 - r^n)\) gives \(S_n = \dfrac{a(1 - r^n)}{1 - r}\) for \(r \ne 1\). Taking \(n \to \infty\), \(\lim_{n \to \infty} r^n = 0\) holds if and only if \(|r| < 1\), yielding \(S_\infty = \dfrac{a}{1 - r}\).

Find the sum of the first \( 10 \) terms of \( 2,5,8,\dots \)

\[ S_{10}=\frac{10}{2}\big(4+27\big)=155. \]

label.en: Worked example — Geometric series & sum to infinity

body.en:
A geometric series has first term 12 and common ratio \(\tfrac{2}{3}\). Find (a) the 5th term, (b) \(S_\infty\).

(a) \(u_5=12\cdot(\tfrac{2}{3})^4=12\cdot\tfrac{16}{81}=\tfrac{64}{27}\).

(b) \(S_\infty=\dfrac{12}{1-\tfrac{2}{3}}=\dfrac{12}{\tfrac{1}{3}}=36\).

label.en: Worked Example C — Series & the Binomial Theorem (Easy Application)

body.en:
Problem (Easy): A geometric progression \( (M_{z}) \) has initial term \( M_1 = 11 \) and common ratio \( r = 2 \). Find the exact value of the fifth term \( M_5 \).

Step-by-Step Solution: Using \( M_5 = M_1 r^4 \), we get \( 11 \times 16 = 176 \).

label.en: Worked Example D — Series & the Binomial Theorem (Medium Application)

body.en:
Problem (Medium): An arithmetic progression \( (R_{m}) \) has first term \( R_1 = 12 \) and common difference \( d = 13 \). Find the exact value of the term \( R_{5} \).

Step-by-Step Solution: Using \( R_n = R_1 + (n - 1)d \), we have \( R_{5} = 12 + (5 - 1)(13) = 64 \).

label.en: ▲ Exam Pacing & Verification Strategy — Series & the Binomial Theorem

body.en: Binomial Validity Shortcut (Cambridge International AS Level (9709 Paper 1 / Paper 4 / Paper 5)): When asked for the range of \(x\) for which the expansion of \((a + bx)^n\) is valid, write \(\left|\dfrac{bx}{a}\right| < 1 \implies |x| < \left|\dfrac{a}{b}\right|\). If multiplying two expansions, take the intersection (smaller radius) of the two validity intervals.

question.en: In an arithmetic progression, the 3rd term is \(14\) and the 7th term is \(34\). (a) Find the first term \(a\) and the common difference \(d\). (b) Find the sum of the first \(25\) terms.

solution.en:
(a) Use \(u_n = a + (n - 1)d\): \[u_3 = a + 2d = 14\] \[u_7 = a + 6d = 34\] Subtract the first equation from the second: \(4d = 20 \Rightarrow d = 5\).
Substitute back: \(a + 2(5) = 14 \Rightarrow a = 4\).
(b) Use the sum formula \(S_n = \tfrac{n}{2}\left(2a + (n - 1)d\right)\) with \(n = 25\): \[S_{25} = \dfrac{25}{2}\left(2(4) + 24(5)\right) = \dfrac{25}{2}(8 + 120) = \dfrac{25}{2}(128) = 25 \times 64 = 1600\]
